references.text: Jesus introduces the parable in verse 16 as a response to the warning against greed in Luke 12:15, where he says: "Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; for one's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions."
Proverbs 11:28 warns: "Those who trust in riches will fall." The parable of the rich man illustrates precisely this danger of relying on material abundance.
Ecclesiastes 5:10 says that whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with it. The rich farmer's constant desire to gather more illustrates this emptiness.
Job 31:24–25 describes the temptation to place one's trust in gold and riches. The parable of the rich farmer shows the consequence of doing exactly that.
Deuteronomy 8:11–14 warns Israel that when they experience abundance and prosperity, they must not forget the Lord their God. The rich farmer forgets God when his fields yield a bountiful harvest.
Hosea 2:8 speaks of how Israel did not recognize that it was God who gave them grain, wine, and oil. The rich man's land produced abundant fruit, but he gave no glory to God.

James 4:13–14 warns against planning the future without considering God's will, and reminds us that life is like a mist that appears for a little while—a theme reflected in the rich farmer's self-confidence.
1 Timothy 6:17 instructs the rich not to set their hope on uncertain riches, but on God. The parable illustrates precisely the danger of relying on earthly wealth.
Psalm 49:6–7 says that no one can buy their way out of death with their wealth. The parable of the rich farmer reinforces this same message.
Psalm 39:7 says: "Like a shadow, man wanders about; in vain they toil and gather up riches, not knowing who will get them." This summarizes the situation of the rich farmer.
Ecclesiastes 2:4–6 describes the Preacher's great projects and accumulation of wealth, but concludes that everything is vanity. The rich farmer's abundance of crops recalls this.
